title: Three perfect days in New York, from the Bowery to the harbor
dek: Brancusi's studio rebuilt at MoMA, the New York Comedy Festival's opening weekend, Wynton Marsalis above Columbus Circle and a free ferry past the Statue of Liberty at dusk.

hero.caption: The Statue of Liberty, seen best for free from the Staten Island Ferry on a short November afternoon.

intro:
The first weekend after the clocks go back is when New York settles into its indoor season. The marathon has come and gone, the Halloween costumes are packed away, and the holiday crowds have not yet arrived. The light fades before 5 p.m., so this plan keeps the afternoons for museums and views and the evenings for comedy, jazz and long dinners.

There is plenty to plan around. The **New York Comedy Festival** opens on Friday, November 6, with more than 200 comedians in over 100 shows across the five boroughs through November 15. At MoMA, **Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio** opened on October 25, reconstructing the Paris studio the sculptor shaped over four decades, with pieces rarely lent by the Centre Pompidou. Downtown, the rebuilt New Museum on the Bowery, reopened in March with an OMA-designed addition, has a fall show about its own street, *The Bowery: Devil's Mile*. Wynton Marsalis leads the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra on Friday and Saturday, and in Brooklyn, Spike Lee opens a new film festival at BAM.

The three days stay close together. Friday is the Lower East Side, from smoked fish to a tenement tour to a vegetable tasting menu. Saturday runs through Midtown to Lincoln Center. Sunday is Lower Manhattan: the 9/11 Memorial, the last days of Canstruction's can sculptures at Brookfield Place, and the ferry out past Liberty Island and back as the skyline lights up.

days.title: Friday: the Lower East Side and the Bowery
days.intro: Four generations of immigrant New York in a few blocks, a new museum about the Bowery, and the comedy festival's opening night.

stops.name: Russ & Daughters Cafe
stops.text: The sit-down cafe of the appetizing shop that has sold smoked fish on Houston Street since 1920. Order a smoked fish board with a bagel, a side of latkes and an egg cream, and take your time: this is the slow breakfast the rest of the day earns. The cafe takes no reservations and opens at 8:30 a.m., so arriving at the door is the best way to avoid a wait. The original shop at 179 E. Houston St. is the place for takeaway.

stops.name: Tenement Museum
stops.text: A block away, guides lead small groups into restored apartments on Orchard Street, telling the stories of the immigrant and migrant families who lived there. It is history told at the scale of a kitchen table, and it makes the walk around the neighborhood afterward far richer. Tours are $30 and can only be taken with a guide, so book a timed slot. Check in at the visitor center at the corner of Orchard and Delancey at least 10 minutes early. The museum opens at 10 a.m. on Fridays.

stops.name: Katz's Delicatessen
stops.text: The pastrami sandwich, hand-cut and stacked on rye, is the order; tip the cutter and you may get a taste while you wait. This May, Katz's reopened the Ludlow Room, a 68-seat dining room that had been a walk-in refrigerator since 1949, with its own cutter and the old freight scale still in place. Hold on to the ticket you are handed at the door: you pay for everything on it when you leave.

stops.name: New Museum
stops.text: The contemporary art museum reopened in March with a new OMA-designed building beside its stack of offset boxes. This fall's shows include *The Bowery: Devil's Mile*, about four centuries of the street outside, and *Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony*, plus a work by Ho Tzu Nyen built into an elevator. It is open 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Fridays and closed Mondays. Afterward, walk south down the Bowery to see the street the show describes.

stops.name: Dirt Candy
stops.text: Amanda Cohen's vegetable restaurant serves a seasonal five-course tasting menu at a long counter facing the open kitchen, with small bites between courses and a vegan version on request. The Infatuation's 2025 review praised the mushroom course and a palm-sized carrot pizza and called it good value for a special occasion. There is no tipping. Book ahead: Friday counter seats go first.

stops.name: Comedy Cellar
stops.text: Opening night of the comedy festival is the right time for the basement club on MacDougal Street, where big names regularly drop in unannounced among the regulars. Lineups for the weekend are posted late Tuesday. There is a two-item minimum, guests must be 21 or older, and phones are locked away during the show. It is a short taxi ride or a 25-minute walk west from Allen Street.

days.title: Saturday: Midtown to Lincoln Center
days.intro: Brancusi in the morning, the skyline at sunset and big-band jazz above Columbus Circle. Sunset comes before 5 p.m., so book Top of the Rock for the late afternoon.

stops.name: Ess-a-Bagel
stops.text: The Midtown bagel institution moved into a larger flagship this year, a few blocks from its original shop. Get a bagel with cream cheese or lox to eat in, or wrap one up for the 15-minute walk west to MoMA. Saturday mornings bring a line, but it moves. If you are staying at the Algonquin, this is a pleasant walk across town before the museums open.

stops.name: The Museum of Modern Art
stops.text: Go straight to the sixth floor for **Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio**, on view through February 27, which reconstructs the Paris studio Constantin Brancusi treated as a work of art in itself, with sculptures rarely lent from the Centre Pompidou alongside his photographs, films, tools and hand-carved pedestals. Then walk the collection galleries. Adult admission is $30, and MoMA opens at 10:30 a.m. on Saturdays, closing at 5:30 p.m. Book a timed ticket; members fill the first hour.

stops.name: The Bar Room at The Modern
stops.text: The Modern's more casual front room, next door to the museum, serves an à la carte lunch daily from 11:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. under chef Thomas Allan. The tarte flambée and the steak tartare suit a light lunch; the caviar hot dogs are the extravagant signature. It is the easiest good meal in the area on a busy Saturday, and you can book a table for the right time between galleries.

stops.name: Top of the Rock
stops.text: Three decks atop 30 Rockefeller Plaza, the highest fully open to the air on the 70th floor, with the Empire State Building framed to the south and Central Park laid out to the north. A late-afternoon slot gives you daylight, sunset and the city lighting up in one visit. Book a timed ticket online, especially for sunset; SKYLIFT, a revolving glass platform, and The Beam, a re-creation of the 1932 girder photo, are add-ons that run weather permitting.

stops.name: Cafe Fiorello
stops.text: Across Broadway from Lincoln Center since 1974, Fiorello is the dependable pre-show Italian, built around its antipasti bar. Share the chicken parm topped with burrata, or the open-faced lasagna, and keep an eye on the clock: the kitchen is used to getting concertgoers out on time. Reserve, or try for a bar seat. It is about a 10-minute walk to Columbus Circle.

stops.name: Jazz at Lincoln Center: Marsalis' Swinging Cities
stops.text: Wynton Marsalis and the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra play three of his suites written for cities he has come to know, the *Vitoria*, *Shanghai* and *Marciac* suites, in the Rose Theater. There is a pre-concert talk at 6:30 p.m. Keep your ticket stub: it gets you in free to the 10:45 p.m. Late Night Session at Dizzy's Club upstairs, where the windows look over Central Park and a younger band plays into the night.

days.title: Sunday: Tribeca and the tip of Manhattan
days.intro: A slow brunch, an hour of reflection at the World Trade Center site, and the harbor at dusk from the deck of a free ferry.

stops.name: Bubby's
stops.text: A Tribeca brunch fixture at the corner of North Moore Street, open daily from 8 a.m. The towering buttermilk pancakes are what people come for; biscuits with gravy and fried chicken are the savory route, and the coffee keeps coming. Book ahead or arrive near opening; it is a popular Sunday brunch.

stops.name: 9/11 Memorial & Museum
stops.text: The two reflecting pools in the footprints of the Twin Towers are free and open to all; the museum beneath them, among the recovered steel and the personal objects of those who died, deserves at least two hours. It is open 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. (closed Tuesdays), with last entry at 5:30 p.m. Adult tickets are $28. Buy a timed ticket online, and leave time to sit by the pools afterward.

stops.name: Canstruction at Brookfield Place
stops.text: Across West Street, teams from architecture and engineering firms including Arup, Gensler and HOK have built large sculptures entirely out of unopened cans of food, set throughout Brookfield Place and its glass-roofed Winter Garden. It is free, open 10 a.m. to 7 p.m., and closes Monday, November 9, after which every can goes to City Harvest. Bring a few cans of your own to the donation table, and vote for the People's Choice award online.

stops.name: The Odeon
stops.text: The brasserie that brought artists and *Saturday Night Live* to Tribeca when it opened in 1980 still has its terrazzo floors and dark wood. A late lunch here is a Sunday pleasure: French onion soup, the moules frites, or the burger with cheddar and fries, and Harry's hot fudge sundae if you have room. It is a 10-minute walk north from Brookfield Place.

stops.name: Staten Island Ferry
stops.text: The best free ride in New York. Boats leave Whitehall every 30 minutes on weekends and take about 25 minutes each way. Stand on the right side going out for the Statue of Liberty, and on the way back you get the Lower Manhattan skyline coming on as the sun sets. Everyone has to get off at St. George; walk through the terminal and board the next boat back. Ignore anyone selling ferry tickets: there are none.

stops.name: The Dead Rabbit
stops.text: A short walk from the ferry terminal, this Irish bar has two rooms, the Taproom and the Parlor. Order the Irish coffee, made with Teeling whiskey and hand-shaken cream floated on top and dusted with nutmeg, or a properly poured Guinness. It is exactly what you want after a cold harbor crossing.

stops.name: Le Gratin
stops.text: End the weekend at Daniel Boulud's bistro in the Beekman hotel, his take on a Lyonnais bouchon and a good room for a cold night. Order the salade lyonnaise with crispy pork belly and chicken livers, a duck dish, and the gratin dauphinois made to his mother's recipe. If you are staying at the Beekman, look up into the hotel's nine-story Victorian atrium on your way in. Reserve ahead for Sunday.

stay.name: The Beekman, A Thompson Hotel
stay.text: An 1881 red-brick office building turned into a 287-room hotel with one Michelin Key, organized around a glass-roofed central atrium that rises nine floors. Tom Colicchio's Temple Court and Daniel Boulud's Le Gratin are downstairs, which makes Sunday night an elevator ride. It is close to the 9/11 Memorial, the ferry and the Brooklyn Bridge, and a quick subway ride from the Lower East Side.

stay.name: The Algonquin Hotel Times Square, Autograph Collection
stay.text: Home of the Algonquin Round Table, where Dorothy Parker and friends traded barbs after World War I, and freshly finished with a multi-year renovation of its rooms and corridors featuring Al Hirschfeld artwork. It is a short walk to MoMA and Top of the Rock for Saturday, and the Blue Bar is a good place for a martini on Friday. Rooms are on the small side, in the old New York way.

stay.name: citizenM New York Bowery
stay.text: Compact, well-planned rooms with XL beds, wall-to-wall windows and tablet controls, a rooftop bar and some skyline views, a few blocks from the New Museum, Katz's and Russ & Daughters. Friday's itinerary is a walk from the door, and the subway at Bowery or Second Avenue gets you to Midtown and the Financial District quickly.

events.name: New York Comedy Festival
events.when: Fri. Nov. 6 to Sun. Nov. 15, evenings
events.where: Clubs and theaters in all five boroughs
events.text: The 22nd festival opens this weekend with more than 200 comedians in over 100 shows. Weekend picks include Moshe Kasher at the Bell House in Brooklyn on Sunday. Tickets sell on the festival site.

events.name: Marsalis' Swinging Cities
events.when: Fri. and Sat. 7:30 p.m.; talk 6:30 p.m.
events.where: Rose Theater, Jazz at Lincoln Center, Broadway at 60th St
events.text: Wynton Marsalis and the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra perform his *Vitoria*, *Shanghai* and *Marciac* suites. Ticket stubs get free entry to the 10:45 p.m. Late Night Session at Dizzy's Club.

events.name: Playback: The Brooklyn Watch Party opening night, Crooklyn
events.text: Spike Lee's new film festival at BAM opens with his 1994 film *Crooklyn*, introduced by Lee and Nicholas Ma.

events.name: Playback Street Party
events.where: Outside BAM Rose Cinemas, Fort Greene, Brooklyn
events.text: A free street party on the festival's second day, alongside screenings of *Love & Basketball*, *City of God*, *The King of Comedy* and more. RSVP on BAM's site.

events.name: Canstruction's final days
events.when: Daily 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.; closes 6 p.m. Mon. Nov. 9
events.text: Free exhibition of sculptures built from cans of food by design and engineering teams; the cans go to City Harvest. A guided tour runs Saturday at 11 a.m. with Eventbrite registration.

know: **From the airports.** From JFK, take the AirTrain ($8.75) to Jamaica and the E train ($3) into Manhattan; the E takes about 35 to 40 minutes from Jamaica to Midtown, and you can tap the same contactless card at both. Taxis from JFK to Manhattan charge a flat $70 plus surcharges, congestion charges, tolls and tip. From Newark, the AirTrain connects to NJ Transit trains to Penn Station; from LaGuardia, take a taxi or the Q70 LaGuardia Link bus to the Jackson Heights subway hub.

**Paying for transit.** Tap a contactless card or phone at subway turnstiles and bus readers with OMNY; a ride is $3. Use the same card every time, because OMNY caps your fares after 12 paid rides in seven days.

**Short days.** Clocks went back on November 1, and the sun now sets before 5 p.m. Book Top of the Rock and plan the Staten Island Ferry for the late afternoon so you catch dusk, and bring a warm layer for the open-air deck and the ferry.
**Closed days.** The 9/11 Museum is closed Tuesdays and the New Museum Mondays, which does not affect this weekend, but Canstruction ends on Monday, November 9.
**Comedy clubs.** Festival week means big crowds at the clubs. Most have drink minimums, many are 21 and over, and some, including the Comedy Cellar, lock away phones during shows.
**Tipping.** In restaurants, 18 to 20 percent of the pre-tax bill is normal (Dirt Candy is an exception, with no tipping); at bars, a dollar or two a drink; for taxis, 15 to 20 percent.
